Sūrat al-Kahf is Meccan, and it has one hundred and eleven verses according to the Basran count, and ten verses according to the Kufan count.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Praise be to Allah, who has sent down the Book upon His servant﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Allah taught His servants and gave them understanding of how to praise and extol Him for the greatest of His blessings upon them, which is the blessing of Islam, and for what He sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) of the Book, which is the means of their salvation. ﴿And has not made in it any crookedness﴾, that is, not any part of crookedness. Crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in physical things; one says: "There is crookedness in his opinion" and "There is a bend in his staff." The intended meaning is the negation of contradiction and inconsistency from its meanings, and of anything from it falling outside wisdom.

**Qayyiman** (upright, straight), and its being in the accusative is due to a hidden verb whose implied sense is: *He made it qayyiman* (upright). This is because when He negated crookedness from it, He thereby affirmed uprightness for it. The benefit of combining the negation of crookedness with the affirmation of uprightness, when either one alone would suffice, is emphasis. For a thing may be described as upright and witnessed to be so, yet on close examination it is not free of some slight crookedness. Alternatively, *qayyiman* means that it is a guardian over the other Books, confirming them and bearing witness to their soundness.

﴿**Li-yundhira**﴾ *andhara* (to warn) is transitive to two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. Here the text confines itself to one of them, and its original form is *li-yundhira alladhina kafaru* (that He may warn those who disbelieved). ﴿**Ba'san**﴾ means punishment, ﴿**shadidan**﴾ means severe. The reason it confines itself to one of the two objects of *andhara* is that what is warned of is the thing being driven toward, so it confined itself to that.

﴿**Min ladunhu**﴾ means proceeding from Him, from His presence.

﴿**Wa-yubashshira al-mu'minina alladhina ya'malun al-salihati anna lahum**﴾ meaning: that for them, ﴿**ajran hasanan**﴾ meaning a good reward, which is Paradise.

"**Wa-yabshuru**" is the reading of Hamza and Ali (al-Kisa'i), (p-٢٨٦)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 3:

﴿Mākithīna﴾ (abiding) is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) referring to the pronoun of "lahum" (for them). ﴿Fīhi﴾ (therein) refers to the reward, which is the Garden. ﴿Abadan﴾ (forever).

﴿And to warn those who say, "God has taken a son."﴾ He mentioned those being warned (al-mundharin) without the thing they are warned of (al-mundhar bihi), the reverse of the first instance, relying on its having been mentioned earlier.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 5:

﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾ meaning: of the child, or of taking Him one. The sense is that their saying this did not proceed from knowledge, but from excessive ignorance. If you say: God taking a child in itself is impossible, so how is it said, "They have no knowledge of it"? I say: its meaning is, "They have no knowledge of it," because it is not among the things that can be known, owing to its impossibility. And the absence of knowledge of a thing is either due to ignorance of the way that leads to it, or because it is impossible in itself. ﴿Nor do their fathers﴾, the imitators, ﴿have any. Grave is the word﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and it carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said, "How great is the word!" The pronoun in "grave" refers to their saying, "God has taken a child," and it is called a "word" just as they call a qasida by that name. ﴿That comes out of their mouths﴾ is an attribute of "word," conveying the magnification of their audacity in uttering it and bringing it out of their mouths, for many of the reprehensible things that Satan whispers into people's hearts they cannot restrain from uttering, but rather they swallow them in silence; so how much more so with a reprehensible matter like this. ﴿They speak only falsehood﴾: they do not say that except as falsehood. "Falsehood" is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: a saying that is false.

ﷺ-free passage; translate faithfully.

**﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself﴾** — destroying yourself, **﴿following their traces﴾** — i.e., the traces of the disbelievers. He likened himself and them, when they turned away from him and did not believe in him, and what overcame him of grief over their turning away, to a man whose beloved ones have left him; so he falls down in sorrows after their traces and destroys himself out of passion for them and yearning at their separation. **﴿If they do not believe in this discourse﴾** — the Qur'an — **﴿out of grief﴾**: an object of purpose (ḥāl/mafʿūl lahu) meaning: because of the excessive sorrow and grief, and the exaggeration in sorrow and anger.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾, i.e., whatever is fit to be an adornment for it and for its people, of the ornaments of the world and whatever is found pleasing in it, ﴿that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾. And the goodness of deed is abstaining from it (the world) and leaving off being deceived by it.

Then he discouraged inclination toward it by His saying ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it﴾ of this adornment ﴿into barren soil﴾, a smooth earth, ﴿dry﴾, with no vegetation in it, after it had been green and grassy. The meaning: We will return it, after its being inhabited, to ruin by causing living things to die, drying up the plants and trees, and so on.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 9:

When He had mentioned, among the universal signs, the adornment of the earth with what He created upon it of kinds without number, and the removal of all of that as though it had never been, He said: ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the Cave and the Inscription...﴾ meaning: that [matter] is greater than the story of the companions of the Cave and their remaining alive for a long period. The kahf (cave) is the wide hollow in the mountain, and al-raqim (the Inscription) is: the name of their dog, or of their town, or the name of a book written concerning them, or the name of the mountain in which the cave is. ﴿They were among Our signs a wonder.﴾ That is: they were a wondrous sign among Our signs, [the word 'ajaban being] a description by way of the verbal noun (masdar), or [it means] "possessing wonder."

ة﴿Idh﴾ — meaning: "Remember when..." — ﴿when the youths sought refuge in the cave and said, "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself"﴾. That is, mercy from the treasuries of Your mercy, which is forgiveness, provision, and security from enemies. ﴿And prepare for us right guidance in our affair﴾, that is, the path we are upon, of separating from the disbelievers, ﴿rashadan﴾ — so that by means of it we may become rightly guided and rightly guiding. Or, make our affair entirely rashad, as in your saying, "I saw from you a lion" (asadan). Or, make easy for us the way to Your pleasure.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 11:

﴿So We struck over their ears in the cave﴾ meaning: We placed over them a veil of sleep. That is, We made them sleep a heavy sleep, in which sounds would not wake them, so the object, which is the veil, has been omitted. ﴿for a number of years﴾ meaning: possessing a number, so ʿadadan (a number) is an adjective of sinīn (years). Al-Zajjaj said: That is, they are counted as a number because of their abundance, for a small quantity is known in its measure without counting, but when it is large it is counted. As for ﴿dirhaman maʿdūdatan﴾ ("counted dirhams"), it refers to a small quantity, because they used to count small amounts and weigh large amounts. (p-288)

Then We roused them (ثُمَّ بَعَثْناهُمْ), that is, We woke them from sleep (أيْقَظْناهم مِنَ النَوْمِ), ﴿that We might know which of the two parties﴾ (لِنَعْلَمَ أيُّ الحِزْبَيْنِ), the two disputing groups among them (المُخْتَلِفَيْنِ مِنهم), regarding the length of their stay (في مُدَّةِ لُبْثِهِمْ). For when they awoke, they disagreed about that, as indicated by His words: ﴿One of them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained"﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Those who said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained" [al-Kahf: 19] were those who knew that their stay had been prolonged, or "which of the two parties," the disputing ones, was from among others (أوْ "أيُّ الحِزْبَيْنِ" المُخْتَلِفَيْنِ مِن غَيْرِهِمْ). ﴿The one who best computes the term of their stay﴾ (أحْصى لِما لَبِثُوا أمَدًا): "the term" (غايَةً). "Aḥṣā" (أحْصى) is a past-tense verb, and "amadan" (أمَدًا) is either an adverb of time governed by "aḥṣā" or a direct object. The past-tense verb is the predicate of the subject, which is "ayyu" (أيُّ); the subject together with its predicate stands in place of the two objects of "naʿlama" (نَعْلَمَ). The meaning is: which of them was most precise in computing "the term" (أمَدًا) of their periods of stay, and most comprehensive in knowledge of the duration of their stay. As for one who says that "aḥṣā" is an elative (أفْعَلُ) from "iḥṣāʾ" (الإحْصاءِ), meaning counting, he has erred, because its formation from other than the bare triliteral is not analogical (لَيْسَ بِقِياسٍ). He said "that We might know" even though He, exalted is He, has never ceased to know that; the intended meaning is what knowledge relates to, namely the manifestation of the matter to them, so that they might increase in faith and reflection, and so that it might be a grace (لُطْفًا) for the believers of their time and a clear sign for its disbelievers. Or the intended meaning is: that We might know their disagreement as an existing fact, just as We knew it before its existence.

We relate to you their story with truth. Indeed, they were youths (fityah), plural of fata (fata), and al-futuwwah (chivalry, the manly virtue of youth) is giving generously, withholding harm, not complaining, avoiding what is forbidden, and practicing noble qualities. It is said: the fata is one who does not claim (a virtue) before the act, and does not praise himself after the act. They believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance, (meaning) in certainty. They were among the close companions of Daqyanus. God cast faith into their hearts, and they feared one another, and they said: let two of us go out alone, two by two, so that each reveals to his companion what he conceals; they did so, and their agreement upon faith was thereby achieved.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 14:

﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾; and We fortified them with patience in leaving their homelands and fleeing with their religion to some of the caves, and We emboldened them to stand up for the word of truth and to openly display Islam. ﴿When they stood up﴾ before the tyrant, who was Decius (Diqyanus), without any regard for him, when he rebuked them for abandoning the worship of idols, ﴿and they said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, boasting, ﴿We will never call upon any god besides Him﴾; and even if we were to name them gods, ﴿we would have uttered an excessive (shatata) saying﴾, that is, a saying of great excess. Shatat is the extreme of injustice and going far in it, from shatta yashhutu and yashuttu: meaning, it went far away.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 15:

﴿هَؤُلاءِ﴾ (These) is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). ﴿قَوْمُنا﴾ (our people) is an ʿatf bayan (explicative apposition). ﴿اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِهِ آلِهَةً﴾ (have taken besides Him gods) is the khabar (predicate). It is an informative statement carrying the meaning of denunciation. ﴿لَوْلا يَأْتُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (Why do they not bring upon them) means: هَلّا يَأْتُونَ عَلى عِبادَتِهِمْ (why do they not bring [proof] for their worship), and the mudaf (the noun "worship") has been elided. ﴿بِسُلْطانٍ بَيِّنٍ﴾ (with clear authority) means: بِحُجَّةٍ ظاهِرَةٍ (with manifest proof). This is a rebuke, because bringing an authority for the worship of idols is impossible. ﴿فَمَن أظْلَمُ مِمَّنِ افْتَرى عَلى اللهِ كَذِبًا﴾ (Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God) by attributing a partner to Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 16:

﴿And when you withdraw from them﴾ is an address from some of them to others, when their resolve was fixed on fleeing with their religion. ﴿And what they worship﴾ is in the accusative as a conjunction (ʿatf) with the pronoun (ḍamīr), meaning: and when you withdraw from them and withdraw from what they worship. ﴿Except Allah﴾ is an exception that is either connected (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), because they used to acknowledge the Creator while associating others with Him, like the people of Mecca; or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: and when you withdraw from the disbelievers and the idols that they worship besides Allah. Or it is a parenthetical statement (kalām muʿtariḍ), an informative statement from Allah Most High about the youths, that they did not worship anything other than Allah. ﴿So take refuge in the cave﴾ — go to it and make the cave your shelter. ﴿Your Lord will spread for you of His mercy﴾ — of His provision. ﴿And will facilitate for you in your affair a means of ease﴾ — (mirfaqan) with a fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the fāʾ, read by Madani and Shami, and it is that by which one derives benefit, meaning: that by which one is aided. They only said this out of confidence in Allah's bounty, strength in their hope due to their reliance upon Him, and the clarity of their certainty; or a prophet in their era informed them of it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 17:

﴿And you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾ — read with the letter zāy lightened (takhfīf): Kūfans read "tazāwaru" (tazawwaru in Shāmī reading), while others read "tazzāwaru." Its origin is "tatazāwaru," which is lightened either by assimilating the tā' into the zāy or by deleting it. All of these derive from zawar (zawar), which is inclination (al-mayl), and from it comes zārahu, meaning he inclined toward him. Al-zūr is inclination away from truth (al-ṣidq). ﴿away from their cave﴾ means it inclines away from it, so its rays do not fall upon them. ﴿to the right﴾ means the direction of the right, and its real meaning is the direction called the right. ﴿And when it sets, it passes them on the left﴾ — taqriḍuhum means it cuts them off, i.e., leaves them and turns away from them. ﴿while they are in a spacious place of it﴾ means in a wide open part of the cave. The meaning is that they are in shade throughout the entire day: the sun does not strike them at its rising or its setting, even though they are in a wide, open place exposed to the sun's rays, were it not that God screens it from them. It was also said: a spacious area of their cave, where the breath of air and the coolness of the breeze reach them, and they do not feel the distress of the cave. ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾ means that what God did to them, namely the sun's turning away and passing them by as it rises and sets, is one of the signs of God. That is, the place in that direction, which the sun would normally strike, is not struck by it, and they are singled out for honour. It was also said: the door of the cave faces north, facing the Bear (banāt Naʿsh), so they are always in shade. The meaning of ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾ is that their condition and their story are among the signs of God. ﴿Whomever God guides, he is the one guided﴾, like what passed in "Subḥān" (glory be). This is praise of them, that they strove for God and submitted their faces to Him, so He guided them to attain that lofty honour. ﴿And whomever He leaves astray, you will never find for him a protecting friend who guides him﴾, i.e., whomever God leads astray, there is no guide for him.

﴿And you would think them﴾ is read with a fatha on the sin by al-Shami (Ibn 'Amir), Hamzah and 'Asim, except al-A'mash. This is an address to everyone. ﴿Awake﴾ is the plural of yaqiz (wakeful). ﴿While they are asleep﴾ means they are sleeping. It was said that their eyes were open while they slept, so the observer would think them awake because of this. ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left﴾: it was said that they were turned twice a year, and it was said that they were turned once, on the day of 'Ashura'. (p. 291) ﴿And their dog stretched out its two forelegs﴾ is a narration of a past state, because the active participle (ism al-fa'il) does not govern when it has the meaning of the past. ﴿At the threshold﴾ means at the courtyard or at the doorstep. ﴿If you had looked upon them﴾ means if you had come upon them and looked at them. ﴿You would have turned away from them﴾ means you would have turned away from them and fled from them. ﴿In flight﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), because the meaning of "you turned away from them" is "you fled from them." ﴿And you would have been filled with dread of them﴾ is read with a shaddah on the lam by the Hijazis, for emphasis. ﴿With terror﴾ is a specification (tamyiz). It is read with a damma on the 'ayn by al-Shami and 'Ali, and it is the fear that strikes the chest, that is, fills it. This is because of the awe that Allah clothed them in, or because of the length of their nails and hair and the largeness of their bodies. It is related from Mu'awiyah that he went out to fight the Romans and passed by the cave, and he said, "I want to enter it." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said, "It has been said about one who is better than you: ﴿You would have turned away from them in flight﴾." So a group entered by his order, and a wind burned them.

[Commentary of al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, p. 292]

﴿And thus We raised them up﴾. Just as We caused them to sleep that sleep, so We awakened them, to demonstrate the power to cause sleep and to raise up, both together. ﴿That they might question one another﴾: so that some of them might ask others, and learn their own condition and what Allah had done with them, so that they might take warning, reflect on the greatness of Allah's power, increase in certainty, and give thanks for the blessing Allah had bestowed upon them. ﴿A speaker among them said﴾: their leader. ﴿How long have you remained?﴾: what is the length of your stay? ﴿They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ This answer was based on a strong presumption (*ghalib al-zann*), and in it is evidence for the permissibility of *ijtihad* (independent reasoned judgment, the exertion of effort to reach a conclusion) and of speaking on the basis of a strong presumption. ﴿They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾ This was a rebuke to them from some of their own number, as if they had come to know, through evidences or through inspiration, that the period was long and that its exact length is known only to Allah. It is also narrated that they had entered the cave in the morning, and they awoke after midday, so they supposed that they were still within their same day. When they saw the length of their nails and their hair, they said this. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, used this verse as evidence that the correct view is that their number was seven. For the speaker said in the verse, ﴿A speaker among them said: How long have you remained?﴾, and this is one person. They then answered him with "We have remained a day or part of a day," and *yawm* in this phrasing is plural in form, and the minimum plural is three. Then He said, ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾, and this is the statement of another group. Thus they become seven. ﴿So send one of you﴾: as if they had said, "Your Lord knows best about that; there is no way for you to know it. So turn to something else that concerns you. Send one of you," that is, Tamlikha. ﴿With this silver of yours﴾: *wariq* is silver, whether minted or unminted. Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Abu Bakr read *wariq* with a sukun on the *ra'*. ﴿To the city﴾: this is Tarsus. Their carrying silver when they fled is evidence that carrying provision and what is suitable for a traveller is the opinion of those who put their trust in Allah, not of those who rely on chance or on what is in the possession of others. It is related of some scholars that he had an intense longing for the House of Allah, and would say, "There are only two things for this journey: a well-saddled mount and trust in the Most Merciful." ﴿Then let him look to which of them﴾: *ayyuha* means which of its people; the noun is elided, as in ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. *Ayyu* is a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿more pure﴾: more lawful, better, more abundant, and cheaper. ﴿Food﴾ is a *tamyiz* (specification). ﴿Let him bring you provision from it, and let him be gentle﴾: let him take care to be gentle in what he undertakes of the transaction, so that he is not cheated, or in concealing himself, so that he is not recognised. ﴿And let him not make anyone aware of you﴾: and let him not do anything that leads to people becoming aware of us, even without intending to. This is called "making aware" because he is the cause of it.

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed they﴾ refers back to the people (ahl) implied in ﴿ayyuhā﴾ (which of them). ﴿If they gain the upper hand over you﴾ means they come to know of you. ﴿They will stone you﴾ means they will kill you in the most vile manner. ﴿Or they will return you to their creed﴾ by compulsion; and "return" (al-'awd) in the sense of "becoming" is common in their speech. ﴿And you will never prosper then, ever﴾: idhan indicates a condition, meaning: "And you will never prosper, ever, if you enter into their religion."

(p-293) **﴿And thus did We cause them to be found﴾**, just as We put them to sleep and raised them up, We made them known to people because of the wisdom in that. **﴿So that they might know﴾**, that is, those to whom We made their condition known, **﴿that the promise of Allah﴾**, which is the Resurrection, **﴿is true﴾**, existent, because their state in sleeping and then waking after it (p-293) was like the state of one who dies and is then raised. **﴿And that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾**, for they would take their own case as evidence for the soundness of the Resurrection. **﴿When they disputed﴾** is connected to *a'tharna* (We caused them to be found), meaning: We caused them to be found when the people of that time were disputing **﴿among themselves over their affair﴾**, the affair of their religion, and differing over the reality of the Resurrection. Some of them said, "Only the spirits will be raised, not the bodies," and others said, "The bodies will be raised together with the spirits." So that the disagreement would be removed, and so that it would become clear that bodies will be raised alive, sensate, with their spirits in them, as they were before death. **﴿Then they said﴾**, when Allah had taken the People of the Cave (to Himself), **﴿"Build over them a structure"﴾**, that is, over the entrance of their cave, so that people would not gain access to them, out of protectiveness toward their dust and to preserve it, just as the dust of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was preserved by the enclosure. **﴿Their Lord knows them best﴾** is from the words of the disputants, as if they had discussed their affair, exchanged words about their lineages, their circumstances, and the length of their stay. When they could not reach the reality of that, they said, **﴿"Their Lord knows them best"﴾**. Or it is from the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as a rebuttal to the words of those who went to extremes in the matter. **﴿Those who prevailed over their affair﴾** among the Muslims and their king, who had more right over them and over building over them, said, **﴿"We will surely take﴾** the entrance of the cave **﴿as a place of worship﴾** in which the Muslims would pray and seek blessing from their place.

It is narrated that the people of the Injil (the Gospel) had grown greatly sinful, and their kings had become insolent, until they worshipped idols and were compelled to worship them. Among those who pressed hardest in this was Daqyanus (Decius). He wanted a group of youths from the nobles of his people to adopt polytheism, and threatened them with death. But they refused except to remain steadfast in faith and firm in it. Then they fled to the cave. On the way they passed a dog, which followed them, and they drove it away. Allah then gave it speech, and it said, "What do you want from me? I love the beloved of Allah. Sleep, and I will guard you." It was also said that they passed a shepherd who had a dog, and the dog followed them in their religion. They entered the cave, and Allah struck their ears (with sleep). Before Allah raised them up, a righteous, believing man ruled their city. The people of his kingdom disagreed about the Resurrection, some affirming it and some denying it. The king entered his house, closed its door, put on a hair shirt, sat on ashes, and asked his Lord to make the truth clear to them. Then Allah put into the heart of a man among their shepherds to demolish what had been sealed over the mouth of the cave, so that he could make it an enclosure for his sheep. When the man whom they had sent to buy food entered the city and brought out silver coins, which were from the minting of Daqyanus, they accused him of having found a treasure. They took him to the king, and he related the story to him. The king set out with the people of the city, and they saw them, and they praised Allah for the sign that indicated the Resurrection. Then the youths said to the king, "We entrust you to Allah, and we seek His protection for you from the evil of jinn and mankind." Then they returned to their resting places, and Allah took their souls. The king threw his garments over them and gave orders, and a coffin of gold was made for each of them. But he saw them in a dream disliking gold, so he made the coffins of teak (saj) and built a place of worship (masjid) over the entrance of the cave.

﴿They will say, "They were three, and their fourth was their dog." And they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them their dog," guessing blindly. And they will say, "They were seven, and their eighth was their dog."﴾ The pronoun in "sayyaqūlūna" refers to those among the believers and the People of the Book who debated their story during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about them, and he delayed his answer until it was revealed to him concerning them. So it was revealed as information about what would take place among them of disagreement over their number, and that the one who was correct among them is the one who says, ﴿"They were seven, and their eighth was their dog."﴾

It is narrated that al-Sayyid and al-Aqib and their companions, who were from the people of Najran, were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and the story of the People of the Cave came up. Al-Sayyid, who was a Ya'qubi (Jacobite, a Christian sect), said, "They were three, the fourth of them their dog." Al-Aqib, who was a Nestorian (a Christian sect), said, "They were five, the sixth of them their dog." The Muslims said, "They were seven, and their eighth was their dog." So Allah confirmed the saying of the Muslims. They knew this only through the information of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and what we have mentioned before.

And it is related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that they were seven men whose names were: Yamlikha, Maksalina, Mashlina. These were the companions of the king's right side. On his left was Marnush, Dabarnush and Shadhanush, and he used to consult these six in his affairs. The seventh was the shepherd who joined them when they fled from their king Daqyanus. The name of their city was Afsus, and the name of their dog was Qitmir.

The *sīn* of the future tense (*sīn al-istiqbāl*) enters only on the first verb (*sayaqūlūna*) and not the other two, yet they are included in its ruling, as when you say, "*qad ukrimu wa-unaʿʿimu*" (I will be honored and I will be blessed), intending the sense of expectation for both verbs together. Or the sense of the future (*al-istiqbāl*), which is suitable for *yafʿalu*, is intended. "Thalāthatun" (three) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are three." Likewise "khamsatun" and "sabʿatun." "Rābiʿuhum kalbuhum" (their fourth is their dog) is a nominal clause consisting of a subject and predicate, functioning as an attribute (ṣifa) of "thalāthatun." Likewise "sādisuhum kalbuhum" and "thāminuhum kalbuhum."

"Rajman bil-ghayb" means throwing out a hidden report and bringing it forth, as in His saying, ﴿and they hurl (charges) at the unseen﴾, meaning they bring it. Or "rajm" was placed in the position of "ẓann" (supposition), as if it were said, "a supposition about the unseen." This is because they often said "rajm bil-ẓann" (a throw of supposition) instead of "ẓann" (supposition), until there was no difference left for them between the two expressions.

The *wāw* that enters on the third clause is the *wāw* that enters on a clause functioning as an attribute of an indefinite noun, just as it enters on a clause functioning as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of a definite noun, as in your saying, "A man came to me, and with him was another," and "I passed by Zayd, and in his hand was a sword." Its benefit is to emphasize the attachment of the attribute to the described noun, and to indicate that his being characterized by it is a fixed and established matter. This *wāw* indicates that those who said, ﴿"They were seven, and their eighth was their dog,"﴾ said it on the basis of firm knowledge, and did not hurl charges by supposition as the others did. The evidence for this is that Allah, exalted is He, followed the first two sayings with His words ﴿"hurling at the unseen,"﴾ and followed the third saying with His words ﴿"Say, my Lord knows their number."﴾ That is: say, "My Lord knows their number," and He has already informed you of it by His saying, "seven, and their eighth was their dog." ﴿None knows them except a few.﴾ Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said, "I am one of that few." It was also said that "illā qalīl" (except a few) refers only to a few of the People of the Book. That is: the People of the Book will say about them such and such, and there is no knowledge of that except in a few of them, while most of them speak by conjecture and guesswork.

﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾, meaning, do not dispute with the People of the Book regarding the matter of the People of the Cave, ﴿except with an outward argument﴾, meaning, except a plain dispute that does not go deep into it. This is that you relate to them only what Allah revealed to you, without adding anything, without belittling them, or in the presence of people so that your truthfulness may become evident. ﴿And do not seek a ruling from any of them concerning them﴾, meaning, do not ask any of them about their story with the intent of challenging him, so that he says something and you refute it and expose what he has; nor with the question of one seeking guidance, because Allah, exalted is He, has already guided you by revealing their story to you.

Here is the translation of the passage:

﴿And never say of anything﴾ concerning something you resolve to do, ﴿"Indeed, I will do that"﴾ — that thing — ﴿tomorrow﴾, meaning: in whatever time is yet to come. He did not mean tomorrow specifically.

**Unless God wills** (*illa an yashā'a Allāh*): that you say it, by means of His granting you permission to say it, or: *"And do not say it except with God's will"*, that is, except by His will. This phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: except while attached to the will of God, saying "If God wills."

Al-Zajjaj said its meaning is: "Do not say, 'I will do that,' except with the will of God Most High, because the saying of the speaker, 'I will do that, if God wills,' means: 'I will not do it except by the will of God.'" This is a rebuke of discipline (*nahy ta'dīb*) from God to His Prophet, when the Jews said to the Quraysh, "Ask him about the Spirit, and about the People of the Cave and Dhu'l-Qarnayn." They asked him, and he said, "Come to me tomorrow and I will inform you," and he did not add the exception (*istithnā'*, the qualifying clause "if God wills"). So the revelation was delayed for him until it weighed heavily upon him.

**And remember your Lord** (*wa-dhkur rabbaka*): that is, the will of your Lord, and say, "If God wills" (*in shā' Allāh*). **When you forget** (*idhā nasīta*): when forgetfulness has befallen you regarding that. The meaning is: when you forget the word of exception, then you recall it and make up for it by mentioning it. From al-Ḥasan: "as long as you are in the assembly of remembrance." From Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "even after a year." This is to be understood as making up for the seeking of blessing (*tabarruk*) through the exception. As for an exception that changes a ruling, it is not valid unless it is connected (*muttaṣil*).

It is related that news reached al-Manṣūr that Abū Ḥanīfa, may God have mercy on him, disagreed with Ibn ʿAbbās regarding the detached exception (*al-istithnā' al-munfaṣil*). So he summoned him in order to rebuke him. Abū Ḥanīfa said to him, "This turns back upon you, for you take the pledge of allegiance by oaths. Would you be content that they leave your presence, make an exception, and then rise up against you?" He admired his words and ordered the one who had criticized him to be removed from his presence.

Or its meaning is: remember your Lord with glorification and seeking forgiveness (*tasbīḥ* and *istighfār*) when you forget the word of exception, as a stringent urging to be mindful of it. Or: pray a prayer you have forgotten when you recall it, or: if you forget something, mention it, so that it reminds you of what was forgotten.

**And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer to right guidance than this"** (*wa-qul ʿasā an yahdiyanī rabbī li-aqraba min hādhā rashadan*): that is, if you forget something, remember your Lord. Remembrance of your Lord at the time of forgetting is to say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something other than this forgotten thing, nearer to rectitude than it and more conducive to good and benefit."

"*an yahdinī*" "*in tarani*" "*an yu'tīni*" "*an tu'allimani*": Makkī reads the final *-ī* (yāʾ) in these forms in both states (in pause and in connection). Abū ʿAmr agreed with him, and Madanī reads it in connection (*waṣl*) only.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 25:

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years﴾. He means their remaining in it alive, with their ears struck (i.e., made to sleep), for this period. This is an explanation of what was stated in summary in His words: ﴿So We struck over their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾ [al-Kahf: 11]. "Sinin" (years) is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "thalatha mi'ah" (three hundred), with the numeral in the construct form ("thalathamiati" as "thalatha mi'ati" with the noun in the genitive), according to Hamzah and ʿAli. This is the placing of the plural in the position of the singular in the specification (tamyiz), as in His words: ﴿Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?﴾ [al-Kahf: 103].

﴿And they added nine﴾, i.e., nine years, since the preceding context indicates it. "Tis'an" (nine) is the direct object (maf'ul bihi), because "zada" (to increase) requires two objects, whereas "izdada" (to increase intransitively/reflexively) requires one object.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 18, verse 26:**

﴿Say: "Allah knows best how long they stayed."﴾ That is: He knows better than those who differed about them the length of their stay. "The truth is what He has told you." Or it is a report of the words of the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab), and "Say: Allah knows best" is a rebuttal of them. The majority hold that this is a statement from Allah, glorified and exalted, that they remained in their cave for such-and-such a period.

﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ He mentions His exclusive knowledge of what is hidden in the heavens and the earth and what is concealed in them of the conditions of their inhabitants.

﴿How clearly He sees and hears!﴾ That is: and how clearly He hears. The meaning is: how perfectly He sees every existing thing, and how perfectly He hears every sound!

﴿They have no protector besides Him﴾ for the people of the heavens and the earth, ﴿no one who manages their affairs﴾ ﴿nor does He share His command﴾ in His judgment ﴿with anyone﴾ among them.

"And do not associate" (wa la tushrik) in the prohibitive form is read by Ibn ʿAmir al-Shami (Shami), who said: they used to say to him, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it," so it was said to him...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 27:

﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord.﴾ That is: of the Qur'an. And do not listen to those who babble about it, seeking alteration. For ﴿there is none who can alter His words.﴾ That is: no one is able to change or alter them; only He Himself has the power to do that. ﴿And you will not find any refuge other than Him.﴾ A place of refuge to which you may turn, should you intend such a thing.

And when a group of the leaders of the disbelievers said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), "Send these clients away, namely Suhayb, 'Ammar, Khabbab, Salman, and others of the poor Muslims, until we sit with you," the verse was revealed: ﴿And restrain yourself with those who call upon their Lord﴾

(p-298) Restrain yourself with them and keep yourself firmly with them, ﴿morning and evening﴾, persistent in supplication at all times. Or, "morning" means for seeking success and facilitation, and "evening" means for seeking forgiveness for shortcomings. Or they mean the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. The reading "bil-ghudwah" (in the morning) is that of Ibn 'Amir al-Shami (the Syrian reader). ﴿Desiring His Face﴾ means seeking the pleasure of God. ﴿And do not let your eyes pass beyond them﴾: do not go beyond them. The verb 'adā, when it means "to go beyond," is transitive, but here it is used with 'an because it implies the meaning of nabā (to turn away from, to avert), as in your saying, "his eye turned away from him" (nabat 'anhu 'aynuhu). The benefit of this implicit meaning (tadmīn) is giving the combined sense of both verbs together, and this is stronger than giving a single meaning. ﴿You desire the adornment of the worldly life﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾: whose heart We have made heedless of the remembrance. This is evidence for us that He, the Exalted, is the creator of the acts of His servants. ﴿And he follows his own desire, and his affair has become excess﴾: going beyond the truth.

**Madarik al-Tanzil** (al-Nasafi) on Surah 18, verse 29:

﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord.﴾ That is, Islam or the Qur'an. "The truth" (al-haqq) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is." ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.﴾ That is: the truth has come and the obstacles have been removed, so nothing remains but your own choice for yourselves, whichever path you wish to take, toward salvation or toward destruction. The imperative form and the offer of choice are used because, once a person is empowered to choose either, he is in effect one who is given the choice and commanded to choose whichever of the two paths he wills. Then He mentioned the recompense of those who choose disbelief, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾ (a'tadna), meaning readied, ﴿for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the disbelievers. The context restricts it in this way, just as the literal sense of the command and the choice is set aside by the context. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure surrounds them.﴾ He likened what encompasses them of the Fire to a *suradiq* (an enclosure), which is the chamber that surrounds a tent. Alternatively, it means a smoke that surrounds the disbelievers before they enter the Fire, or a wall of fire that encircles them. ﴿And if they call for relief﴾ from thirst, ﴿they will be relieved with water like *al-muhl*﴾, which is the dregs of oil, or what has been melted from the substances of the earth. There is a mockery of them in this.

﴿It will scald the faces﴾: when it is brought near to be drunk, the face is scorched by its heat.

﴿Wretched is the drink﴾ (p-٢٩٩) ﴿and wretched is the Fire as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]: *murtafaqan* means a reclining place, from *al-rifq* (ease, comfort). This phrasing is for the sake of *mushakalah* (rhetorical correspondence) with His saying ﴿and how good a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]. Otherwise, the people of the Fire have no resting (irtifaq).
Having explained the reward of the one who chose faith, He said: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds—indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good in deed.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 31:

﴿Those, for them are Gardens of Eden﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), an explanation of the vague reward. You may also make "Indeed We do not waste" and "Those" two predicates together, and the intended meaning is "whoever among them has done good deeds," as in your saying: "Samn (clarified butter) is two manes for a dirham." Or, because "whoever does good deeds" and "those who believed and did righteous deeds" are joined by one meaning, he placed "whoever does good deeds" in the position of the pronoun. ﴿Rivers flow beneath them; they will be adorned therein with bracelets﴾: min here indicates the starting point (li'l-ibtida'). The word "asawir" is indefinite; it is the plural of "asawira," which is the plural of "siwar," and it is indefinite to convey the vagueness of its excellence. ﴿Of gold﴾: min here is explanatory (li'l-tabyin). ﴿And they will wear green garments of sundus﴾: sundus is what is thin of brocade (dibaj). ﴿And istabraq﴾: what is thick of it; that is, they combine the two types. ﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾: reclining is singled out because it is the posture of the affluent and of kings upon their beds. ﴿How excellent the reward﴾: the Garden. ﴿And how good a resting place﴾: the Garden and the couches; "murtafaqan" means a place of reclining.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 32:

﴿And set forth for them the parable of two men.﴾ He likened the state of the disbelievers and the believers to the state of two men, who were two brothers among the Children of Israel. One of them was a disbeliever named Qitrus, and the other was a Muslim named Yahudha. It was said that they are the two mentioned in "As-Saffat" in His words: ﴿Said a speaker among them, "Indeed, I had a companion"﴾ [al-Saffat: 51]. They inherited from their father eight thousand dinars, and they divided them into two shares. The disbeliever bought land for a thousand dinars, and the believer said: "O Allah, my brother has bought land for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand," and he gave it in charity. Then his brother built a house for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand," and he gave it in charity. Then his brother married a woman for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I have made a thousand as a dowry for the houris." Then his brother bought servants and goods for a thousand dinars, and he said: "O Allah, I have bought from You the everlasting youths for a thousand," and he gave it in charity. Then he was afflicted with need, so he sat on his brother's path. He passed by him with his retinue, and he confronted him, but he drove him away and rebuked him for squandering his wealth in charity. ﴿We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines﴾, vineyards of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and We made the palms encompass the two gardens. This is something that landowners (dahaqin) prefer for their vineyards: to make them enclosed by fruit-bearing trees. It is said: "hafafuhu" when they surrounded it, and "hafafituhu bihim," meaning I made them surround it. It is transitive to one object, so the preposition "bi" makes the second object. ﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: We made it a land comprising the foods and fruits. He described the cultivation as being continuous and interlaced, with nothing intervening to cut it off, together with a good appearance and an elegant arrangement.

Both gardens yielded their produce, ﴿كِلْتا الجَنَّتَيْنِ آتَتْ﴾ "each of the two gardens gave" its fruit. He used the singular verb (ātat) to agree with the word's form, because the word kilta is grammatically singular. Had he said ātatā, agreeing with the meaning, it would have been permissible. ﴿أُكُلَها﴾ "its produce" means its fruit, ﴿وَلَمْ تَظْلِمْ مِنهُ﴾ "and did not fall short in it" means it did not lose any of its yield, ﴿شَيْئًا﴾ "anything." And We made a river gush forth through the midst of them, ﴿وَفَجَّرْنا خِلالَهُما نَهَرًا﴾. He described them by the completeness of their fruit and the full yield without any deficiency, then by what is the source and foundation of all good, namely the matter of irrigation, so He made it the best thing with which they could be watered, which is the flowing river within them.

﴿And he had fruit﴾ for the owner of the two gardens: types of wealth, from "thamamara maalahu" (he multiplied his wealth), meaning when he increased it. That is, beyond the two described gardens, he had abundant possessions of gold, silver and other things. "Lahu thamar" ("he had fruit") and "wa-uhita bi-thamarihi" ("and it was encompassed by its fruit"): Asim read thamarihi with a fat-ha on the mim and the tha', Abu Amr read it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim, and others read it with a damma on both.

﴿So he said to his companion while he was disputing with him﴾ "yuhawiruhu", meaning he was returning words to him, from "haara yahuru" (he returned). That is, Qatrus took the hand of the Muslim, walking him around the two gardens, showing him what was in them, and boasting to him of the wealth he possessed that the other did not.

﴿I am more numerous than you in wealth and stronger in men﴾: "a'azz nafaran" means more powerful in supporters and retinue, or in sons who are male, because they go out with him, unlike females. (p-301)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 35:

﴿And he entered his garden﴾ — one of his two gardens; or he called them both a "garden" because of the unity of the enclosing wall, and [called them] "two gardens" because of the flowing river between them. ﴿While he was wronging himself﴾ — harming himself by disbelief. ﴿He said: "I do not think that this will ever perish."﴾ — i.e., that this garden would ever be destroyed. He doubted that his garden would perish, because of his long hope (ṭūl al-amal), his persistent heedlessness, and his being deceived by the respite; and you see that the speech of the conditions of most wealthy people among the Muslims bears witness to this.

Surah 18, verse 36 — Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil)

﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾ [happening], ﴿and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a destination﴾. This is an oath from him that, if he were returned to his Lord by way of supposition, as his companion claims, he would surely find in the Hereafter something better than his garden in this world, asserting his honour before Him and his standing with Him. "Munqalaban" is a specification (tamyiz), meaning: a return and an outcome.

Qur'an 18:37: "His companion said to him while he was arguing with him: Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust?"

That is, He created your origin (asl), because the creation of his origin is a cause of his creation, and the creation of his origin was a creation of him. "Then from a drop (nutfah)": that is, He created you from a drop. "Then He fashioned you into a man (rajul)": He made you balanced (adalaka) and perfected you as a human being, a male who had reached maturity, the stage of men. He (the disbelieving man) became a disbeliever in God because of his doubt about the Resurrection.

﴿But I﴾ is read with an alif in pause (waṣl) by the Shāmī reader, while the rest read it without an alif. Adding the alif at a pause (waqf) is agreed upon. Its original form is "لَكِنْ أنا" (lākin ana). The hamzah was dropped and its vowel transferred to the nūn of "لَكِنْ", so the two nūns came together. The first was then assimilated into the second (idghām) after being made quiescent (sukūn). ﴿He is Allah, my Lord﴾: "هُوَ" (huwa) is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the matter is "Allah, my Lord". The sentence is the predicate (khabar) of "أنا" (ana), and the returning pronoun (rājiʿ) connecting it back to the subject is the pronominal suffix "ي" (the yā' of "rabbī"). This is a corrective contrast (istidrāk) to his words "أكَفَرْتَ" (akafarta, "Have you disbelieved?"). He said to his companion: "You are a disbeliever in Allah, but I am a believer and a monotheist," just as one says, "Zayd is absent, but ʿAmr is present." There is an ellipsis (ḥadhf) in it, meaning: "I say, He is Allah." The evidence for this is the conjunction (ʿaṭf) in ﴿and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾.

﴿And why did you not﴾ say, that is, "halla" (why not), ﴿when you entered your garden, say: "What Allah wills [has come to pass]. There is no power except in Allah"﴾ ma is a relative pronoun in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "The matter is what Allah wills." Or it is a conditional in the accusative position, with its response omitted, meaning: "Whatever Allah wills, it comes to be." The meaning is: why did you not say, upon entering it and looking at what Allah had provided you from it, "The matter is what Allah wills," acknowledging that it and everything in it came about by the will of Allah, and that its affair is in His hand: if He wills, He leaves it flourishing, and if He wills, He ruins it. "There is no power except in Allah," affirming that whatever strength you have to build it and manage its affairs is by His assistance and support. Whoever reads ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth﴾ with "aqalla" in the accusative has made "ana" a separating pronoun (fasl, a pronoun that separates the subject from the predicate). Whoever reads it in the nominative, and this is al-Kisa'i, makes "ana" the subject (mubtada'), with "aqallu" as its predicate, and the whole clause is the second object of "tarani" (you see). And in His saying ﴿and offspring﴾ there is support for those who interpreted "nafar" (in His saying ﴿and mightier in manpower﴾) as "children."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 40:

﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ in this world or in the Hereafter. ﴿And send upon it a calamity﴾ (ḥusbān), a punishment ﴿from the sky, so that it becomes a barren ground (ṣaʿīd) slippery (zalaq)﴾, a white land on which one slips because of its smoothness.

Or its water will become sunk into the earth, [so that] you will not be able to find it.

Ghawran: ghā'ir, i.e., going away into the earth. ﴿So you will not be able to find for it any seeking﴾: so its seeking will not be possible for you, let alone its existence. The meaning: if you see me as poorer than you, then I expect from God's making that He will turn what is in me and in you of poverty and wealth, and grant me, for my faith, a garden better than your garden, and strip you of His blessing for your disbelief, and ruin your orchards.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 42:

﴿And his fruit was encompassed﴾ is an expression for its destruction. Its origin is from "the enemy encompassed him" (aḥāṭa bihi al-ʿaduww), because when an enemy encompasses someone, he has taken possession of him and gained control over him; then it came to be used for every kind of destruction. ﴿So he began﴾, i.e., the disbeliever, ﴿wringing his hands﴾, striking one of his palms against the other in regret and anguish. The wringing of the hands became a metaphor (kināya) for regret and anguish, because the one who regrets turns his hands over, back to front, just as he is metaphorically described by biting the hand (ʿaḍḍ al-kaff) and by falling into the hand (suqūṭ fi al-yad). And because it carries the meaning of regret (naḍam), it is followed by the preposition ʿalā, as if it were said: "So he began to regret" ﴿over what he had spent on it﴾, i.e., on its cultivation, ﴿while it lay fallen on its trellises﴾. The meaning is that its trellised vines had collapsed upon their supports, and the vines had fallen on top of them. ﴿And he said, "Oh, would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord!"﴾ He remembered his companion's admonition, so he knew that he had been struck because of his disbelief and rebellion, and he wished that he had not been a polytheist, so that Allah would not have destroyed his garden, when wishing no longer benefited him. It is also possible that this was a repentance from polytheism, a regret for what had been from him, and an entry into faith.

​"And he had no company to help him against Allah" — who could support him (يَقْدِرُونَ عَلى نُصْرَتِهِ) — "other than Allah." That is: He alone is the One able to support him; no one other than Him is able to support him, except that He did not support him for a wisdom (لِحِكْمَةٍ). "And he was not one who could defend himself" — and he was not one who could protect himself by his own strength from the vengeance of Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 44:

﴿There, the guardianship belongs to Allah, the True.﴾ "Yakun" (with the ya') and "al-wilayah" (with a kasra on the waw) are read by Hamzah and ʿAli. Thus, with a fatha, al-wilayah means support and allegiance (al-nusrah wa al-tawalli), and with a kasra it means authority and dominion (al-sultan wa al-mulk). The meaning is: "There," that is, in that station and that state, support belongs to Allah alone; no one else possesses it or is able to provide it apart from Him. This confirms His words, ﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah﴾ [al-Kahf: 43]. Or: "There," authority and dominion belong to Allah, who cannot be overcome. Or: in such a severe situation, Allah is turned to, and every person in distress believes in Him. That is, His words ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 42] were a statement he was forced into, which he uttered out of anguish at what had befallen him from the evil consequence of his disbelief; had it not been for that, he would not have said it. Or: "There," the guardianship belongs to Allah, in which He gives victory to His allies, the believers, over the disbelievers and avenges them. That is, in what He did to the disbeliever, He gave victory to his believing brother and confirmed his words, ﴿It may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a calamity from the heaven﴾ [al-Kahf: 40]. This is supported by His words ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, meaning for His allies. Or "there" refers to the Hereafter: in that abode, guardianship belongs to Allah, like His words ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. "Al-Haqq" with a damma is read by Abu ʿAmr and ʿAli, as an attribute of "al-wilayah," or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is the Truth, or he is the Truth. The others read it with a kasra, as an attribute of "Allah." "ʿUqban" with a sukun on the qaf is read by ʿAsim and Hamzah, and with a damma by the others. In the irregular readings, it is "ʿUqba" on the pattern fuʿla, and all of them mean the same thing: the final outcome (al-ʿaqibah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 45:

﴿And strike for them the parable of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky,﴾ meaning: it is like water which We sent down (p-304) ﴿so that the vegetation of the earth mingles with it﴾, i.e., it grows thick and dense because of it, until some of it mingles with other parts; or, the water affects the plants, so they mingle with it until they are watered. ﴿Then it becomes dry stubble﴾, dry and crumbling; its singular is hashimah (a dry, broken stalk). ﴿Which the winds scatter﴾, i.e., blow away and carry off. "al-Riyah" (the winds) is read by Hamzah and Ali (in the plural form, al-riyah). ﴿And Allah is over all things﴾, of creating and annihilating, ﴿Capable﴾, i.e., Powerful. He compares the state of this world in its freshness and splendour, and what follows it of destruction and annihilation, to the state of vegetation that becomes green, then dries up, and the wind scatters it as though it had never been.

Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world (﴿المالُ والبَنُونَ زِينَةُ الحَياةِ الدُنْيا﴾), not the provision for the grave nor the preparation for the Hereafter. ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾ (al-baqiyat al-salihat) are deeds of goodness whose reward remains for the person, or they are the five daily prayers, or "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah), "al-hamdu lillah" (praise be to Allah), "la ilaha illa Allah" (there is no god but Allah), and "Allahu akbar" (Allah is the Greatest). ﴿Are better in the sight of your Lord for reward﴾ (khayrun 'inda rabbika thawaban), meaning in recompense (jaza'an), ﴿and better in hope﴾ (wa khayrun amalan), because it is a true promise, whereas most hopes are false. The meaning is that its possessor hopes in this world for the reward of Allah, and attains it in the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 47:**

﴿And [mention] the day﴾ — i.e., remember the day ﴿when We set the mountains in motion﴾. "Tusayyar" (the mountains are set in motion) is the reading of Makki, Shami and Abu 'Amr; meaning: they move through the air, or they are carried away, by being made into scattered dust, dispersed particles. ﴿And you see the earth laid bare﴾, having nothing upon it that covers it of what was on it of mountains and trees. ﴿And We gather them﴾, i.e., the dead, ﴿and We leave out none of them﴾. I.e., We do not leave; "ghadara-hu" means he left it, i.e., abandoned it, and from it comes "al-ghadr" (treachery): abandoning fidelity; and "al-ghadir" (a pool): that which the torrent has left behind.

﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in ranks﴾ — lined up, standing out plainly: you will see their assembly just as you see each one of them, with no one hiding another. Their state is likened to the state of soldiers being reviewed before the sultan. ﴿Indeed you have come to Us﴾ — meaning: We will say to them, "You have come to Us." This implied verb may be the governing element of the accusative in "the day We set the mountains in motion" (yawma nusayyir). ﴿Just as We created you the first time﴾ — meaning: We have resurrected you just as We brought you into being the first time; or, "you have come to Us barefoot, naked, with nothing with you, just as We created you at first." He says "wa-ḥasharnāhum" (and We gathered them) in the past tense after "nusayyir" and "wa-tarā" (and you will see) to indicate that their gathering occurs before the setting in motion and before the manifestation, so that they may witness those terrors, as if it were said: "and We had gathered them before that." ﴿Nay, you claimed that We would never appoint for you an appointment﴾ — a time for the fulfilment of what you were promised through the tongues of the prophets concerning resurrection and rising up; or a place of promise for the reckoning.

The Book will be placed (open), meaning the books of deeds; and you will see the criminals fearful (of) what is in it, of sins, and they will say: "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out no small matter nor great, but records it all?" That is: it leaves no sin undone, but has counted it and kept account of it. And they will find what they did present (in the records), ready (to be read), or (they will find) the recompense for what they did. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, by recording against him what he did not do, or by increasing his punishment, or by punishing him without any crime.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 50:

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam,"﴾ a prostration of greeting (taḥiyya) or a prostration of submission (inqiyad). ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn﴾ This is a resumptive clause (mustaʼnaf), as if someone had asked, "What about him, that he did not prostrate?" So it was said, "He was of the jinn." ﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾ he went out from what his Lord had commanded him regarding prostration. This is evidence that he had been commanded to prostrate along with the angels. ﴿Will you then take him﴾ — that is, ﴿and his offspring﴾ — the hamza here is for denunciation and wonder, as if it were said: "After what has come from him, do you take him and his offspring ﴿as allies instead of Me﴾ and exchange Me for them?" Among his offspring: Laqis, the one who whispers during prayer; al-A'war, the one who engages in adultery; Batar, the companion of calamities (al-sa'ib); Mutawwas, the companion of rumors (al-arajif); and Dasim, who enters and eats with those over whom Allah the Exalted is not invoked. ﴿And they are an enemy to you﴾ — enemies. ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ — evil is the substitute from Allah that Iblis is, for whoever substitutes him and obeys him in place of obedience to Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 51:

﴿I did not make them witness⦆ i.e., Iblis and his offspring, ﴿the creation of the heavens and the earth⦆, meaning: (p-306) that you have taken them as partners to Me in worship. They would only be partners in it if they were partners in divinity (al-ilahiyyah). So He negated their sharing in divinity by His saying ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth⦆, so that I might take them as helpers (a'tadida bihim) in creating them, or consult them about it. That is: I alone created things, so single Me out in worship. ﴿Nor the creation of themselves⦆, i.e., nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others, like His saying "and do not kill yourselves" (Qur'an 4:29). ﴿And I was not one who takes the misleaders⦆, i.e., I was not one who takes them ﴿as helpers ('adudan)⦆, i.e., aides. He placed "the misleaders" in the position of the pronoun, to censure them for misguiding. Since they were not helpers to Me in creation, what is wrong with you that you take them as partners to Me in worship?

ﷻ﴿And the Day He says﴾ (Allah says to the disbelievers; Hamzah reads it with the nun, "We say"), ﴿"Call upon My partners whom you claimed"﴾ — ﴿nādū﴾ means "call out" (ud'ū), i.e., call with a loud voice — ﴿"that they were among you as My partners, so that they may protect you from My punishment."﴾ By "partners" He means the jinn, and He attributed the partners to Himself according to their assumption, as a rebuke to them. ﴿So they called upon them, but they did not respond to them, and We placed between them a mawbiq﴾ — a place of destruction, from waqaba, yabiqu, wubūqan, meaning "he perished"; or it is a verbal noun like "mawʿid" (appointment). That is: ﴿"And We placed between them"﴾ a valley from the valleys of Hell, which is a place of destruction and severe punishment, shared by them, in which they all perish together; or [the mawbiq is] between them and the angels, ʿUzayr and ʿIsā. And al-mawbiq is a far-off barrier, that is: We placed between them a great distance, because they are at the bottom of Hell while they [the worshipped ones] are in the highest of the Gardens.

And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain (فَظَنُّوا, literally "they thought," here meaning they were certain) that they are going to fall into it (﴿أنَّهم مُواقِعُوها﴾), that is, they will be mixed into it and fall within it, and they will find no escape from the Fire (﴿وَلَمْ يَجِدُوا عَنْها﴾), that is, from the Fire, no turning away (مَصْرِفًا), no way of escape (مَعْدِلًا).

The Qur'anic verse quoted is ﴿And We have indeed diversified in this Qur'an for mankind every kind of example﴾ that they need, ﴿but man is most of all things given to dispute﴾.

"Tamyiz" (specification, a grammatical accusative clarifying a noun) here: "most of all things" means: most of the things from which disputation arises, if you enumerate them one by one, [namely] contention and quarrelsome argument for falsehood. That is to say: the disputatiousness of man is greater than the disputatiousness of every other thing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 55:

﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them﴾, i.e., its cause, which is the Book and the Messenger, ﴿and from asking their Lord for forgiveness, except that the way of the ancients should come upon them, or that the punishment should come upon them﴾. The first "أنْ" is in the accusative case (naṣb), and the second is in the nominative case (rafʿ), and before it there is an omitted genitive-construction noun (muḍāf maḥdhūf, a noun in an idafa construction that is left out). Its estimated form is: "And nothing prevented the people from faith and seeking forgiveness except the waiting for the way of the ancients to come upon them, which is destruction, or the waiting for the punishment to come upon them," i.e., the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿Qubulan﴾ is the reading of Kufan (Kūfī, the reader of the Kufan school), i.e., "kinds," the plural of qabīl. The rest read "قِبَلًا" (qibalan), i.e., "face to face."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 56:

﴿And We do not send the messengers except as bearers of good news and warners.﴾ It is halted upon (waqf) at this point and resumed (isti'naf) with His words: ﴿But those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood﴾, meaning their saying to the messengers: "You are nothing but mortals like us, and if God had willed, He would have sent down angels," and the like. ﴿So that they may refute the truth thereby﴾: that they may remove and nullify prophethood through disputation. ﴿And they take My signs﴾: the Qur'an. ﴿And that with which they are warned﴾: "ma" here is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the returning pronoun from the relative clause is omitted, meaning: "and that which they were warned of, of punishment." Or it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: "their warning." ﴿As a mockery﴾: a place of ridicule (istihza'). With the zay and the hamza silent (hazah): Hamzah. With the hamza replaced by a waw (huzwan): Hafs. With a damma on the zay and the hamza (huzuan): the others.

[The passage begins mid-commentary, at the words "by the Qur'an."]

by the Qur'an. For this reason the pronoun (ḍamīr) refers back to it in masculine form in His words ﴿that they understand it﴾ and ﴿so he turned away from it﴾. [This means] he did not take heed when he was reminded and did not reflect. ﴿And forgets what his hands have sent forward﴾: the consequence of what his hands have sent forward of disbelief and sins, without contemplating it or considering that the evildoer and the doer of good must each receive a recompense. Then He gave the reason for their turning away and forgetfulness, namely that they have been sealed upon their hearts, in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, meaning veils, the plural of kinān, which is the covering, ﴿lest they understand it, and in their ears a heaviness﴾, meaning a weight that prevents them from hearing the truth. It is plural after the singular in keeping with the wording of "man" (who), though its meaning is plural. ﴿And if you call them﴾, O Muhammad (p-٣٠٨) ﴿to guidance﴾, meaning to faith, ﴿they will never be guided﴾, so there will never be any guidance from them whatsoever. ﴿Then﴾ is a conditional response and answer, which indicates the negation of their being guided by the Messenger's call. The sense is that they made what should have been the cause of attaining guidance into a cause of its absence. It is also said that it is the Messenger's answer to an implied statement, as if he had said: "Why should I not call them, out of eagerness for their Islam?" and so it was said: "And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, then," ﴿ever﴾, for the entire span of legal responsibility.

Your Lord is the All-Forgiving, abounding in forgiveness, Possessor of mercy, characterized by mercy. ﴿Were He to take them to task for what they have earned, He would hasten their punishment.﴾ That is: and it is of His mercy that He does not immediately call the people of Makkah to account, despite their extreme enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿But for them there is an appointed time﴾, which is the Day of Badr, ﴿and they will never find, other than Him, any refuge﴾ (mawill), meaning a place of escape or shelter. It is said: "wa-ala" (وَأَلَ) when one escapes, and "wa-ala ilayhi" (وَأَلَ إلَيْهِ) when one seeks refuge in him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 59:

﴿Wa-tilka﴾ (And those) is a subject (mubtada'), ﴿al-qura﴾ (the towns) is an attribute (sifah), because demonstrative nouns (asma' al-isharah) are described by generic nouns (asma' al-ajnas), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿ahlaknahum﴾ (We destroyed them). Or ﴿tilka al-qura﴾ (those towns) is in the accusative (nasb) by supposing a verb "ahlakna" (We destroyed), by way of the rule of exegetical elaboration (shari'at al-tafsir). The meaning is: "And those are the people of the towns." What is intended is the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud. ﴿Lamma zalamu﴾ (when they did wrong) is like the wrongdoing of the people of Makkah. ﴿Wa-ja'alna li-mahlikihim mau'idan﴾ (and We appointed for their destruction a fixed time) means: We set for their destruction a known time, from which they will not be delayed, just as We set for the people of Makkah the Day of Badr. Al-mahlik means the act of destruction and its time, with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam by Hafs, and with a fatha on both by Abu Bakr, meaning: for the time of their destruction, or for their destruction. Al-mau'id is either a time or a verbal noun (masdar).

And [mention] when ﴿Moses said to his young companion﴾. He is Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn. He was called *fatāh* (young companion) because he served Moses, followed him, and took knowledge from him. ﴿I will not cease﴾ means I will not stop. The predicate is omitted, because the situation and the context indicate it. As for the first, the omission is because it was a journey. As for the second, the omission is because His words ﴿until I reach the junction of the two seas﴾ set a limit, which requires something to be the limit for him. So the meaning must be: "I will not cease to travel until I reach the junction of the two seas," which is the place where Moses was promised a meeting with al-Khiḍr, peace be upon them both. It is the meeting point of the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome. He was called Khiḍr because wherever he prayed, the ground around him turned green. ﴿Or I will journey for a long age﴾ means or I will travel for a long time. It was said that this was eighty years. It is narrated that when Moses, peace be upon him, prevailed over Egypt with the Children of Israel, and they settled there after the destruction of the Qibṭ (Copts), he asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just in judgment?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow desire." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people in addition to his own knowledge, perhaps he will hear a word that guides to guidance or turns him away from destruction." He said: "If there is among Your servants someone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "More knowledgeable than you is al-Khiḍr." He said: "Where shall I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, by the rock." He said: "My Lord, how can I find him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket, and wherever you lose the fish, he is there." So he said to his young companion: "When you lose the fish, inform me." They set out walking, and Moses fell asleep. The fish moved, and it fell into the sea. When the time for the midday meal came, Moses asked for the fish, and his young companion informed him that it had fallen into the sea. They came to the rock, and there was a man covered with his garment. Moses greeted him, and he said: "And how is greeting in our land?" Then he made himself known to him, and he said: "O Moses, I have knowledge that Allah taught me, which you do not know, and you have knowledge that Allah taught you, which I do not know."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 18, verse 61:

﴿So when they reached the meeting place of the two of them﴾: the meeting place of the two seas. ﴿they forgot their fish﴾: meaning, one of them forgot it, and he was Yūsha' (Joshua), because he was the one in charge of the provisions and his guide. ﴿So I forgot the fish﴾ [al-Kahf: 63]. This is like their saying, "They forgot their provisions," and it is the one who is responsible for the provisions who forgets them. It is said that the fish was a salted fish. They stopped for a night beside the shore of the Spring of Life (ʿAyn al-Ḥayah), and Mūsā (Moses) slept. When the spirit and coolness of the water touched the fish, it came back to life and fell into the water. ﴿And it took its way into the sea﴾, meaning it made for itself a path from the land to the sea. ﴿Tunnelling (sarab)﴾: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning it tunnelled (sariba) into it, sarab, that is, it entered into it and hid itself in it. (p-310)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 62:

﴿So when they had passed beyond it﴾ the meeting-place of the two seas, then they halted, having traveled as far as God willed. ﴿Moses said to his young man: "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours."﴾ Nasab means weariness. He had not grown tired, nor had he been hungry before that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 63:

﴿He said: "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock..."﴾ It is the place of the appointment. ﴿Indeed, I forgot the fish﴾ Then he made an excuse, saying, ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan﴾ — and Hafs reads it with a ḍammah on the hā' (ﷺ)... ﴿except Satan﴾ by casting thoughts into the heart. ﴿That I should mention it﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the hā' in "ansanīhu," meaning: and none caused me to forget its mention except Satan. ﴿And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner﴾ — namely, that its trace remained to wherever it went.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 64:

﴿He said: "That is what we were seeking."﴾ [نَبْغِ, nabgh], i.e., we were seeking (نَطْلُبُ). With the yā' (ي) it is read by Makki, and Abu 'Amr and 'Ali agreed with him; and Madani (in pause/connection) [in the wasl]. Without a yā' in both places, following the orthography of the Mushaf (اتِّباعًا لِخَطِّ المُصْحَفِ). That (ذَلِكَ) is a reference to taking the way (اتِّخاذِهِ سَبِيلًا), i.e., "that which we were seeking," because the disappearance of the fish was a sign (عَلَمًا) for meeting al-Khidr, peace be upon him. ﴿So they turned back, retracing their footsteps﴾, i.e., they returned along the path by which they had come. ﴿Retracing (qasas)﴾ — they followed their traces (يَقُصّانِ قَصَصًا), i.e., they followed their footprints closely. Al-Zajjaj said: "Qasas is following a trail (اتِّباعُ الأثَرِ)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 65:

﴿So they found a servant from among Our servants﴾: that is, al-Khidr, lying asleep beneath a garment, or sitting in the sea. ﴿We had given him mercy from Us﴾: it is revelation and prophethood, or knowledge, or long life. ﴿And We had taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾: it means the reporting of unseen matters. It has been said: "ladunni knowledge" (al-'ilm al-ladunni, knowledge bestowed directly from God) is that which comes to the servant by way of inspiration (ilham).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 66:

﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you on the condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, right guidance?"﴾ That is: knowledge that carries right guidance (rushd), by which I may be guided in my religion. "Rashadan" (رَشَدًا) is read by Abu 'Amr, and both are dialectal forms (lughatan), like al-bukhl and al-bakhal (both meaning stinginess). In it is evidence that one should not abandon the pursuit of knowledge even if one has reached its utmost limit, and that one should show humility before whoever is more knowledgeable than oneself.

Said [Musa]: "Indeed you will not be able to have patience with me." (In the reading of Hafs, the yā' in "maʿiya" is vowelled with a fatḥa, and likewise what follows it in the surah.) "Patience" means: refraining from denunciation and questioning.

﴿And how can you be patient about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ *Tamyīz* (a grammatical term for an accusative noun that specifies or clarifies what precedes it). Here the word is *khubran*. He denied the ability to be patient with him, using emphatic phrasing (*ʿalā wajh al-taʾkīd*, for emphasis), and gave as the reason that he undertakes matters which, outwardly, are objectionable (*manākīr*, sing. *munkar*). A righteous man cannot restrain himself from being distressed when he sees such things, so how much more so if he is a prophet?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 69:

﴿He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey any order of yours."﴾ Patient (ṣābiran) among the patient, refraining from denial and objection. ﴿And I will not disobey any order of yours﴾: it is in the position of accusative (naṣb) by conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon ṣābiran, that is: "You will find me patient and not disobeying." Or it is a conjunction upon "you will find me" (satajidunī), and it has no grammatical position (lā maḥalla lahu).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 70:

﴿Said he: "If you follow me, then do not question me﴾ with fath on the lam and tashdid on the nun is (the reading) of Madani and Shami; and with sukun on the lam and takhfif on the nun is (the reading) of the others. The yā' is present in both by consensus ﴿about anything until I myself mention it to you﴾.
